name: Rectifier
description: A rectifier tube: a hot cathode in the middle, an anode on each side. Each anode is on its own AC power supply, a sine of period 20 whose amplitude you set; the right one's runs half a period behind the left one's. Electrons flow from the cathode to an anode only while that anode is positive: the tube conducts one way. The cathode is connected to ground through a load resistor (30) and a capacitor (1): losing electrons, it charges positive, and its potential is the rectifier's output, DC from AC. Make a smooth supply: the cathode's mean potential between 8.5 and 11.5, and its ripple (half its peak-to-peak) below 1.2, over $t = 40$ to $80$.

reality.represents: A full-wave rectifier tube with a smoothing capacitor

remarks.detail: Electrons flow to an anode only while it is above the cathode, so two anodes on opposite phases charge the output on both halves of the cycle: full-wave rectification, as in the twin-anode rectifiers of old power supplies.

remarks.line: The ripple of an RC filter
remarks.detail: The capacitor holds the output between the peaks and the load drains it: the ripple falls as RC grows.
Supplies, resistors, capacitors and coils are ideal lumped parts, per unit length of the tube; they drive the electrodes and feel the current the electrons induce (Ramo).

The tube is the same all along its length: its electrodes are long prisms, its electrons long lines of charge, its currents per unit length. A real tube is a few centimetres long and has end effects; the textbooks' planar and coaxial laws assume this symmetry too.

The cathode gives off as many electrons as its field pulls off (the space-charge limit), released at rest. A real hot cathode emits them with thermal energies of about 0.1 eV, which lets a little current flow against a small retarding field and moves the potential's minimum slightly out from its face.

electrodes.label: cathode (hot; the output, through R and C to ground)
right anode (AC supply, half a period behind)
